message.content:
Lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) belong to two very different mammalian orders—Carnivora and Perissodactyla, respectively. Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of the two clades, which lies within the larger Laurasiatherian super‑clade.

**In short:**  
The common ancestor of a lion and a zebra is a Laurasiatherian mammal that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago, before the split that gave rise to the distinct lineages of carnivores (like lions) and odd‑toed ungulates (like zebras).

There's no function relevant. So we just answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) is the last common ancestor of the family Felidae and Equidae. That would be a common ancestor in the order Carnivora? Wait, zebra is in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). Lion is in order Carnivora. They diverged earlier. The common ancestor would be a mammalian ancestor, perhaps the last common ancestor of all placental mammals? Actually lion and zebra are both mammals but belong to different orders. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the ancestor of the clade Eutheria. But if we want a more specific common ancestor, it's the last common ancestor of the clades Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the common ancestor is a Laurasiatherian ancestor. So answer: The last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the clades Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is a Laurasiatherian mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. So we can say: The common ancestor is a Laurasiatherian mammal from the late Cretaceous/Eocene. So answer accordingly.
